extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science; general readers interested in comparative party systems
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style political-science analysis that defines and classifies 'professional' (Inner Circle) and 'non‑professional' (Outer Circle) politicians in the United States, describes their traits, sizes, and causes for the composition of the political class, and lists reasons why the 'best men' avoid politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of the Inner Circle (professional politicians)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the Inner Circle, that is to say, the persons who make political work the chief business of life, for the time being, includes: — First. All members of both Houses of Congress. Secondly. All Federal office-holders except the judges, who are irremovable, and the 'classified civil service.' Thirdly. A large part of the members of State legislatures.... Fourthly. Nearly all State office-holders, excluding all judges in a very few States, and many of the judges in the rest. Fifthly. Nearly all holders of paid offices in the greater and in many of the smaller cities, and many holders of paid offices in the counties. Sixthly. A large number of people who hold no office but want to get one, or perhaps even who desire work under a municipality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage enumerates categories (federal, state, local office-holders, expectants) and notes variation by State; gives estimates and explains that 'work' of politics centers on winning nominations and elections. The author cautions the line between professional and non-professional is indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'political work' in America
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The "work" of politics means in America the business of winning nominations (of which more anon) and elections,'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that this political work is 'incomparably heavier and more complex than in England' and is the basis for assessing who is a professional politician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why political work is heavier/more complex in the U.S. (six reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because: (1) The voters are a larger proportion of the population; (2) The government is more complex (Federal, State, and local), and the places filled by election are therefore far more numerous; (3) Elections come at shorter intervals; (4) The machinery of nominating candidates is far more complete and intricate; (5) The methods of fighting elections require more technical knowledge and skill; (6) Ordinary private citizens do less election work, seeing that they are busier than in England, and the professionals exist to do it for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numbered list is offered as the explanation for why US politics requires more sustained professional effort; it functions as a set of evaluative criteria for when political activity becomes 'professional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator: proportion of Outer Circle vs Inner Circle as a measure of political health
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The proportion between Outer Circle and Inner Circle men is in the United States a sort of ozonometer by which the purity and healthiness of the political atmosphere may be tested.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author identifies regions where Outer Circle is largest (New England, country parts of New York, Northern Ohio, North-western States) and where professionals most abound (great cities). Use of this proportion is presented as a diagnostic criterion of political quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile of the 'ward politician' (humbler/professional type)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ward politician' usually begins as a saloon or bar-keeper, lodging-house keeper, low-grade lawyer, or after failure in store-keeping; education typically only elementary; politics mean a scramble for places or jobs; often 'vulgar, sometimes brutal... associates of criminals.' They form groups to reach and control ignorant voters and 'pack meetings with their creatures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes social origin, typical occupations, limited political comprehension, methods (control of ignorant or immigrant voters), and that this type 'thrives best in cities, and even in the most crowded parts of cities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile of minor politicians in smaller cities and country
rubrics_metrics.description: In smaller cities and in the country the minor politicians are mostly native Americans, petty lawyers, officials, people who turned office-seekers, with a fair sprinkling of store-keepers, farmers, and newspaper men; the great majority have some regular avocation and are not wholly professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with ward politicians: more respectable, more regularly employed, law as the business that best fits politics; still often 'a sordid and selfish view of politics and a laxity, sometimes amounting to fraud, in the use of electioneering methods.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile of upper-level party managers and leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Above the rank-and-file stand the officers in the political army, the party managers, including the members of Congress and chief men in the State legislatures, and the editors of influential newspapers. Many have pushed up from humbler ranks; others are men of superior ability and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes them as often devoting whole time to political work, drawing income from politics, coming more from poorer and less cultivated ranks, but often proficient in popular oratory, electioneering, and party management; mixture of 'clean and unclean' characters acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to estimate size of the political (Inner Circle) class
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimation by counting offices and 'expectants': e.g., about 100,000 Federal offices attractive to aspirants; assuming one expectant per office and scaling State/local offices as 1.5 times Federal yields an estimate (illustratively) over 500,000, and after adjustments a 'very large total, doubtless over 250,000 of persons whose chief occupation and livelihood lies in politics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides arithmetic reasoning and caveats (deduct persons who don't make politics their main business); offered as an empirical approach to quantify the professional political class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and definition of the Outer Circle (non‑professional politicians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outer Circle politicians are those who work for their party without desiring office; their action in the main consists in voting, and the ordinary native citizen does this more steadily and intelligently than anywhere in Europe. The American Outer Circle comes nearer to including the whole nation than does the Outer Circle of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical examples (Abolitionists, Lincoln) and explains Outer Circle as the influence that 'counterworks' professionals via public opinion and frequent ballots; described as important check on professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons the 'best men' do not go into politics (causal criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several constitutional and social causes: lack of a social/commercial capital (no Paris/London attraction), absence of a class with hereditary claim to public office, rotation and precariousness in congressional careers (a man cannot easily re-enter Congress by another door), politics less interesting (absence of large foreign or constitutional questions), division of legislative authority (Federal vs State narrows opportunities), more attractive openings in business (railways, finance), lack of social prizes attached to office in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each point is explained with comparative examples (Britain/France/Switzerland) and used to account for why able citizens hesitate to embrace political life; presented as explanatory criteria rather than normative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of press roughness and 'bad company' as deterrents
rubrics_metrics.description: The roughness of politics, exposure to misrepresentation, invective and a reckless press are acknowledged but judged 'insignificant' as the principal reason best men avoid politics; author argues that in every country politicians face similar exposures and that organization of the party system is a more important deterrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides reasoning: public shrewdness, examples that even in decorous countries politicians must disregard abuse, and the claim that party-organization difficulties and humiliations at the initial stages are greater factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical virtues and vices ascribed to American professional politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: They show a high average level of practical cleverness and versatility, often some legal knowledge; usually correct in life regarding intoxication and sexual immorality, but often charged with 'a low tone, with laxity in pecuniary matters, with a propensity to commit or to excuse jobs, with a deficient sense of the dignity which public office confers and the responsibility it implies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes validity of charges will be discussed later and acknowledges many 'brilliant exceptions' and 'leading politicians whose honour is as stainless' as Europe's best; thus this operates as a balanced evaluative profile.
